newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine mourners fly to Falklands war graves.
newsitem.headline: Argentine mourners fly to Falklands war graves.

text.p: Relatives of Argentine troops buried in the Falkland Islands left Buenos Aires for the South Atlantic archipelago on Wednesday to visit war graves on the first of two such trips planned this year.

The 15 mourners accompanied by a Catholic priest were seen off from Buenos Aires' Aeroparque airport by chanting veterans of the 1982 war over the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and says were usurped by Britain in 1833.

They had arrived at the military section of the airport in a bus painted with an image of the islands superimposed on the blue and white Argentine flag, over the motto: "Nobody will change our destiny. Long live our motherland!"

But Argentine Deputy Foreign Minister Andres Cisneros told local radio that politics should be kept out of the event. "It would be inappropriate for the islanders or ourselves to use the family visits for political ends."

Veterans' leader Cesar Trejo, who helped organise the trip for five mothers, two fathers, one widow and seven brothers and sisters of fallen Argentine servicemen, described it as a "spiritual and emotional necessity for those who until now have not been able to pay homage to their loved ones."

Argentine Catholic priest Guillermo Constantini will lead the mourners in a service at a cemetery containing the graves of 234 men, many identified only as "Conscripto" (Conscript) or "Soldado" (Soldier). On 123 crosses are written the words "An Argentine soldier known unto God."

The service will be out of view of residents of Darwin and neighbouring Goose Green, scene of some of the worst fighting of the Falklands war in which some 1,000 servicemen, mostly Argentines, died. Another group of 15 will visit in February.
Previous such visits took place in 1986, 1991 and 1995, but the fiercely pro-British islanders are bitterly opposed to the presence of Argentine mourners.

They remain deeply mistrustful of Argentina despite the resumption of diplomatic ties between Britain and Argentina in 1989 and a rapprochement that has included visits to Argentina by British royals and the rapid expansion of trade links.
Many Falklanders would like to see the Argentine soldiers' remains moved to the mainland. But for Argentine war veterans, the graves are a symbol of their country's territorial claim.

"The presence of the bodies of the fallen in the territory is testimony to Argentina's will to recover the islands," Trejo said. "It was also the desire of those who died there, according to what they told their families in letters from the battlefield."
